medium.conteudo_html:
Can AI Really Understand Faith? Some Questions and Criticisms About a Bahá’í Marriage Platform I Built

A few months ago, I built ashna.date, a Bahá’í dating and marriage platform that uses AI-assisted profiles and semantic matching.

I’ve seen some skepticism about using AI in something as personal as faith and marriage. I think many of these concerns are reasonable, and I wanted to explain how the platform actually works, what the technology can and cannot do, and why I made certain design choices.

I’m the developer, so naturally I have my own perspective. But I also recognize that building something doesn’t automatically make its design right.

1. Can AI measure someone’s spirituality or sensitivity to the Holy Spirit?

I don’t think it can, and I wouldn’t claim that it does.

AI cannot reliably measure someone’s closeness to God, sincerity of faith, spiritual maturity, or sensitivity to the Holy Spirit.

These are deeply personal qualities that cannot be established through a few written answers.

What ashna.date does is considerably more modest. It asks people five open-ended questions about how they live their faith, their approach to service, what they believe makes a marriage work, how they deal with difficulties, and what they would want a future spouse to understand about them.

The system compares similarities in what people have expressed. It doesn’t assign anyone a spiritual worth or rank people according to how good a Bahá’í they are.

2. Does using AI mean the profiles are artificial?

The people behind the profiles are people who have signed up and submitted their own information and answers.

They describe their experiences of faith, their values, their hopes for marriage, and sometimes quite personal aspects of their lives.

AI helps turn those answers into readable introductions.

I understand why someone might feel uncomfortable with AI writing part of a personal profile. An AI-generated introduction can sound polished, and that may raise questions about authenticity.

But the underlying material comes from what members themselves have shared.

We should also be careful about what can actually be verified. The platform does not independently verify every person’s identity, religious affiliation, or the truth of everything they submit.

The introduction is a representation of their answers, and like any representation, it may be incomplete.

Regardless of the technology involved, I believe the people sharing those experiences deserve to be treated as individuals, with dignity and respect.

3. Is AI judging people’s personalities or character?

This is an important distinction, and I think some of my earlier descriptions of the platform could have been more precise.

After the AI produces an introduction, another model converts that text into a numerical representation called an embedding.

The system compares these embeddings to identify similarities in language and meaning.

For example, two people might express related views about community service, consultation, family responsibilities, or marriage, even if they use different words.

That similarity can be useful for discovering profiles worth reading.

But a numerical representation of someone’s written answers is not a measurement of their character.

It cannot establish whether someone is honest, compassionate, patient, or capable of sustaining a marriage.

Those qualities are far more complex than what can be inferred from a short profile.

4. Why use AI at all? Why not let people write their own profiles?

The main reason is consistency.

Everyone answers the same five open-ended questions, and AI helps turn those answers into a consistent profile format. This also provides a more standardized textual basis for semantic matching.

The content still comes from what each person chooses to share.

For transparency, the actual profile-writing prompt includes these instructions:

Use their own words and be specific. Be honest but kind — this is someone putting themselves forward sincerely. Keep it simple and direct. Never mention what they didn’t say. No analysis, no clinical language, no bullet lists.

The current default profile-writing model is Grok, developed by xAI. For semantic matching, the platform uses Google’s Gemini embedding technology.

Of course, AI can still omit nuance, change emphasis, or misrepresent something. A prompt cannot guarantee perfect accuracy.

That’s a limitation worth acknowledging.

5. Does a higher similarity score mean two people are more compatible for marriage?

It means their written profiles have a higher degree of semantic similarity according to the model.

It doesn’t establish that they will have a successful relationship.

Two people can share many values and still be incompatible in practice. Others may differ significantly in personality or life experience and still build a strong marriage.

The matching system is a discovery tool. Its results are possible introductions, not predictions of marital success.

6. What about the star map? Is it ranking people’s spiritual qualities?

The star map is a visual representation of similarities between profiles.

Each star represents a member, and profiles with related patterns of meaning may appear near one another.

It is simply a way to explore the community visually.

The position of a star doesn’t indicate someone’s spiritual development, moral worth, or desirability as a spouse.

And because complex information is compressed into a two-dimensional map, the visual distances are approximate.

7. Should technology have this much influence over something as personal as marriage?

I think this is probably the most important question.

There are legitimate concerns about how recommendation systems shape what people see and whom they encounter. A platform’s design can influence opportunities for connection, even when it leaves the final decision to users.

I don’t think technology should claim authority over deeply personal decisions.

On ashna.date, people decide which profiles interest them, whom they wish to contact, what they want to ask, and whether a relationship is worth pursuing.

AI can help people discover potential connections, but it cannot determine what a person should value in a spouse or whether two people should marry.

Those decisions belong to the people involved.

8. Why build something specifically for Bahá’ís?

Marriage can involve questions of faith, service, family, community, and shared expectations about life.

For people seeking a Bahá’í marriage, these subjects may be especially relevant.

The idea behind ashna.date was to create a place where people could describe how they actually live and understand their faith, and meet others who may be exploring similar questions.

There are many different experiences and perspectives among Bahá’ís, and I wouldn’t want a matching algorithm to define what an ideal Bahá’í or ideal marriage looks like.

The platform is simply one additional way for people to find one another.

I realize that some people may still be uncomfortable with AI being involved in dating and marriage, and I respect that.

There are reasonable questions about privacy, representation, algorithmic bias, and whether technology can meaningfully support human relationships.

I don’t have definitive answers to all of them.

Building ashna.date has also made me more conscious of the distinction between what AI can calculate and what it can genuinely tell us about another human being.

I think the technology has some practical value in helping people discover one another, while its limitations deserve to be discussed openly.

The people behind these profiles have their own lives, experiences, beliefs, and hopes for marriage. Whatever someone thinks about the technology, I hope that human dimension remains part of the conversation.

I’m happy to answer questions about the implementation, the AI prompts, or the decisions behind the platform. Constructive criticism is welcome.

medium.titulo: Nuxt 前端框架，還有 Server Middleware？從 HTTP 安全標頭開始和 nosniff
medium.resumo: 使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫
medium.conteudo_html:
使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫

最近在處理 Nuxt 網站的安全性設定時

Nuxt 明明是前端框架

卻可以透過 server/middleware 修改伺服器回傳的 HTTP Header？

原來 Nuxt 不只是 Vue 的前端開發工具，它也具備伺服器端的執行能力

Nuxt 不只是前端框架

在一般 Vue SPA（Single Page Application）中

伺服器主要提供 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript 檔案

瀏覽器下載後，再由 JavaScript 產生畫面

Nuxt 則支援 SSR（Server-Side Rendering，伺服器端渲染）。

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  ssr: true
})

當 SSR 啟用時

Nuxt 可以先在伺服器執行 Vue 程式、產生 HTML，再傳送給瀏覽器。

瀏覽器收到 HTML 後，會再透過 JavaScript 接手互動功能

這個過程稱為 Hydration。

因此 Nuxt 的程式可能在兩個不同環境執行：

  • Server（伺服器）：產生 HTML、處理 HTTP 請求。
  • Client（瀏覽器）：呈現畫面、處理使用者互動。

Nuxt 使用的伺服器引擎叫做 Nitro

它可以處理 SSR、Server API 和 Server Middleware。

Middleware 是什麼？

Middleware 中文稱為「中介軟體」。

可以把它想成辦公大樓的警衛。

當有人準備進入辦公室時，警衛會先檢查身分，確認符合條件才讓他進去。

Middleware 也是類似的概念

在主要處理流程之前，先執行某些工作。

Nuxt 有兩種容易搞混的 Middleware。

Route Middleware

放在：middleware/

主要處理頁面導航

例如檢查使用者是否登入。

export default defineNuxtRouteMiddleware((to) => {
  const isLoggedIn = false

  if (!isLoggedIn && to.path !== '/login') {
    return navigateTo('/login')
  }
})

Server Middleware

放在：server/middleware/

主要處理進入 Nitro 的 HTTP 請求

例如記錄請求資訊、設定 HTTP Response Header。

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(event, 'X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
})

兩者最大的差別是：

  • Route Middleware：處理使用者要前往哪個頁面。
  • Server Middleware：處理伺服器收到的 HTTP 請求。

為什麼需要 X-Content-Type-Options？

當瀏覽器向伺服器索取檔案時

伺服器會透過 Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器檔案類型。

Content-Type: text/html
Content-Type: application/javascript
Content-Type: text/css

但某些情況下，瀏覽器可能根據檔案內容自行猜測類型。

這種行為稱為 MIME Sniffing。

伺服器回傳：

Content-Type: text/plain

但檔案內容卻是：

alert("Hello!")

伺服器宣告這是普通文字，但內容看起來像 JavaScript。

如果瀏覽器在載入腳本時自行猜測類型並執行，就可能增加安全風險。

因此可以設定：

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

要求瀏覽器在載入 JavaScript、CSS 等資源時，遵守對應的 MIME 類型檢查。

如果宣告的類型不符合要求，瀏覽器就會阻擋載入，而不是自行猜測後繼續使用。

使用 Server Middleware 設定安全標頭

在 Nuxt 專案建立：

server/middleware/security-headers.ts

import {
  defineEventHandler,
  setResponseHeader
} from 'h3'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(
    event,
    'X-Content-Type-Options',
    'nosniff'
  )
})

這段程式其實只做一件事情：

在 Nuxt 伺服器處理 HTTP 請求時，替回應加入 X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff。

逐行來看：

  • defineEventHandler()：建立一個 HTTP 請求處理函式。
  • event：代表這次 HTTP 請求與回應的相關資訊。
  • setResponseHeader()：替 HTTP 回應設定 Header。
  • X-Content-Type-Options：安全標頭名稱。
  • nosniff：要求瀏覽器遵守對應資源的 MIME 類型限制。

因為檔案放在 server/middleware/，Nuxt 會自動註冊這段程式。

不需要在每個 Vue 頁面重複設定。

不過要注意，這個 Middleware 只能影響經過 Nitro 處理的 HTTP 回應。

如果正式環境還有 IIS、Nginx 或其他 Web Server 直接提供檔案，就需要另外確認。

如何驗證設定成功？

啟動 Nuxt 專案後，可以使用 Chrome 開發者工具確認。

  1. 按下 F12 開啟 DevTools。
  2. 選擇 Network。
  3. 重新整理網頁。
  4. 點選網頁的 Document 請求。
  5. 查看 Response Headers。
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

這代表目前檢查的 HTTP 回應已經包含安全標頭。

另外，也應檢查 JavaScript 和 CSS 是否具有正確的 Content-Type

避免新增 nosniff 後造成檔案載入失敗。

重點整理

  • Nuxt 不只是前端工具，也具備透過 Nitro 執行伺服器端程式的能力。
  • SSR 可以在伺服器先產生 HTML，再交由瀏覽器接手互動。
  • Route Middleware 負責頁面導航與路由檢查。
  • Server Middleware 負責 Nuxt 伺服器端的 HTTP 請求處理。
  • Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器回應內容的類型。
  • MIME Sniffing 是瀏覽器根據內容自行判斷檔案類型的行為。
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff 可以降低特定資源因 MIME 類型錯誤判斷而產生的安全風險。
  • 設定完成後，仍需要檢查 HTTP 回應，確認標頭確實生效。

medium.titulo: Why Do We Even Need React, Vue and Angular? 6 Things They Do So You Don’t Have To
medium.resumo: In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself.
medium.conteudo_html:
In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself. What they add is knowing when to call them, which ones to use, and which calls to skip.

Open the source of React, Vue or Angular and you won’t find any browser magic. They create elements with document.createElement, change text with nodeValue and textContent, and attach listeners with addEventListener, exactly like you would in a plain .js file.

So why does almost every team reach for one of them? It isn’t because the DOM is slow or because vanilla JavaScript can’t build a real app. These libraries make a long list of small decisions for you, on every click, and they get them right every time. You would get most of them right too, at least on the first day. By month six, with three teammates and forty screens, you’d be getting them wrong.

Here are the six that matter most. I checked each one against the shipped source of React 19.3, Vue 3.5 and Angular 21.2, and measured the browser side in Chrome 156. The interactive version of this post, with live demos you can run in your browser, is on allahabadi.dev.

1. You stop updating the screen by hand

This is the big one, and every other point in this post sits on top of it.

Take a small shopping cart. A cart icon shows a count, a list shows the items, a line shows the total, and the checkout button says how many items you’re buying. Four places on the screen show the same piece of data.

Without a library, every action has to remember every place:

<span id="badge">0</span>
<ul id="list"></ul>
<b id="total">0</b>
<button id="checkout">Checkout (0)</button>
const cart = [];
const badge = document.querySelector('#badge');
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const total = document.querySelector('#total');
const checkout = document.querySelector('#checkout');
function addItem(item) {
  cart.push(item);
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = `${item.name} ₹${item.price}`;
  list.append(li);
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function removeLast() {
  cart.pop();
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.lastElementChild?.remove();
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  // checkout.textContent was never updated here
}

Nothing in that code crashes. removeLast just forgets the checkout button, so after you remove an item the button still says the old number. No error shows up in the console, and no test fails unless someone wrote one for that exact label. A real app has hundreds of these "update these four things" functions, and each new feature adds one more place each of them has to remember.

The fix is to flip the direction. Instead of writing “when this happens, change these elements”, you write one function that says what the screen should look like for any cart, and you call it after every change:

let cart = [];
function render() {
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.replaceChildren(...cart.map((i) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `${i.name} ₹${i.price}`;
    return li;
  }));
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function addItem(item) { cart = [...cart, item]; render(); }
function removeLast() { cart = cart.slice(0, -1); render(); }

(It uses the same four const elements as the first snippet.) Now no action can forget the button, because no action touches the screen at all. They change the data, and render draws the screen from it. People describe this as UI is a function of state: same state in, same screen out.

That is the whole idea React, Vue and Angular are built on. In React the same cart looks like this:

import { useState } from 'react';
export function Cart() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  return (
    <>
      <span>{cart.length}</span>
      <ul>
        {cart.map((i, n) => <li key={n}>{i.name} ₹{i.price}</li>)}
      </ul>
      <b>{total}</b>
      <button onClick={() => setCart([...cart, { name: 'Tea', price: 40 }])}>Add tea</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCart(cart.slice(0, -1))}>Remove last</button>
      <button>Checkout ({cart.length})</button>
    </>
  );
}

But my vanilla render() has a cost the React version doesn't. It rebuilds the whole list on every click, even when only one item changed. Do that on a list of 2,000 rows and the browser throws away 2,000 elements and builds 2,000 new ones to change one price. Doing "render from state" without paying that price is the actual work these libraries do, and the next three sections are about how they do it.

2. They pick the right moment to touch the DOM

A browser tab runs your JavaScript and draws the page on the same thread. It can’t paint while your code is running. Roughly, one turn of the loop looks like this: run a task (your click handler), run the microtasks queued during it, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then recalculate styles, lay the page out and paint.

When you change the DOM directly, the change happens right there, in the middle of your handler. When you then read something that depends on layout (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), innerText), the browser has to stop and lay the page out right now, because the layout it has is out of date. Do that in a loop and you get one full layout per pass. This has a name: layout thrashing.

const rows = document.querySelectorAll('.row');
const heights = [];
for (const row of rows) {
  row.textContent = 'Read';        // write: layout is now out of date
  heights.push(row.offsetHeight);  // read: browser must lay out right now
}

The libraries never write to the DOM the moment you change state. They write it down and do all the DOM work later, in one go:

  • React collects every setState call made during an event. If your click handler calls setName, setCity and setAge, React renders once and commits once, after your handler returns and before the browser paints. Work that isn't urgent, like a startTransition update, goes through React's scheduler, which posts its work with MessageChannel and gives the main thread back every 5 ms so a keypress doesn't have to wait for a long render.
  • Vue puts each component that needs updating in a queue and flushes the whole queue in one microtask (Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs)). That is why you need await nextTick() to see the updated DOM right after changing state.
  • Angular in zoneless mode schedules change detection with whichever fires first, a setTimeout or a requestAnimationFrame, so a burst of changes in one handler leads to one check.

The core of the trick fits in six lines:

let queued = false;
function scheduleRender(render) {
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  queueMicrotask(() => { queued = false; render(); });
}

Call scheduleRender(render) ten times in one click and render runs once.

One correction to something you’ll often read: none of the three uses requestIdleCallback to apply your updates. An idle callback can be delayed for a long time, and an update needs to be on screen in the next frame. Vue uses it for hydrateOnIdle, and Angular for @defer (on idle) blocks. Both are cases where waiting is fine.

You can do all of this by hand. You’d have to know that layout reads in a loop are expensive, that a microtask runs before the next paint, and that requestAnimationFrame exists. Then you'd have to make sure every developer on the team knows it as well, in every file.

3. They choose the fast DOM API for you

The DOM often gives you two ways to do the same thing, and one of them costs a lot more. The best-known pair is textContent and innerText.

textContent joins up the text nodes inside an element. It never looks at CSS. innerText returns the text as it appears on screen: it leaves out elements hidden with CSS, applies text-transform, and turns line boxes into line breaks. To know what is on screen, the browser needs up-to-date styles and layout. So reading innerText right after you changed something forces a full layout.

Writing is a different story, and this is where the usual advice gets it half wrong. In my traces, setting innerText did not force layout. It cost about the same as setting textContent. The only difference is that the innerText setter turns \n into <br> elements. The expensive part is reading it.

The read is easy to put in a hot loop without noticing, like this search filter:

const query = 'error';
for (const row of document.querySelectorAll('.row')) {
  row.hidden = !row.innerText.includes(query);
}

Setting row.hidden makes the layout out of date, and the next row's innerText needs it to be current, so the browser lays the page out again for every row. Swap innerText for textContent and that loop doesn't do any layout until the frame is painted.

Here is how React sets text on an element, from react-dom 19.3 (lightly reformatted):

function setTextContent(node, text) {
  if (text) {
    var firstChild = node.firstChild;
    if (firstChild && firstChild === node.lastChild && 3 === firstChild.nodeType) {
      firstChild.nodeValue = text;
      return;
    }
  }
  node.textContent = text;
}

If the element already holds exactly one text node, React changes that node’s nodeValue in place, which is the cheapest text write the DOM has. Otherwise it uses textContent. innerText doesn't appear anywhere in that path.

Most of the time, these libraries don’t read the DOM at all. The current cart, the current name and the current filter all live in JavaScript, in React’s fibers, Vue’s reactive objects or Angular’s views. When your code reads row.innerText to find out what a row says, it asks the browser to work it out from the page. A library already knows, because it rendered that row. Fewer reads means fewer chances to force layout, and you don't need to remember which layout-reading APIs are dangerous. I measured more than 40 of them in another post.

They skip updates that change nothing

Say a price on the screen is 499, and your code sets it to 499 again. Nothing on screen changes. Does the browser notice?

I tested it in Chrome 156 on a page with 3,000 paragraphs. Each test wrote the same value 200 times and read offsetWidth after each write, the way real code often measures right after updating:

  • el.textContent = '499' (same value): 200 layouts. textContent replaces the child text node with a brand new one every time, so the browser treats it as new content.
  • el.innerHTML = '499' (same value): 200 layouts, for the same reason, plus an HTML parse each time.
  • textNode.nodeValue = '499' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome sees that nothing changed. A MutationObserver still received all 200 records, though.
  • el.style.width = '50px' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome skips an identical inline style too.
  • if (el.textContent !== '499') el.textContent = '499': 0 layouts, 0 mutations.

So the browser skips some identical writes and redoes others, and the two most common ways of setting text are the ones it redoes. You’d have to know which is which.

const price = document.querySelector('#price');
for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
  price.textContent = '499';
  price.offsetWidth;
}

All three libraries put the check in front of the DOM, so they never need that list:

  • React compares old and new text before it marks a text node for update (current.memoizedProps !== newProps). One level up, if you call setCount(5) while the count is already 5, Object.is says nothing changed and React can skip rendering that component altogether.
  • Vue’s reactive setter runs hasChanged(value, oldValue) first. Assigning the same value to a ref doesn't trigger anything that depends on it.
  • Angular compares every template binding to its previous value with Object.is (bindingUpdated) and only touches the DOM when it differs.

All three compare with Object.is, so they check "is it the same value", not "does it look the same":

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
Object.is(user, user);              // true:  update skipped
Object.is(user, { name: 'Asha' });  // false: treated as a change

That is why in React you create a new object to trigger an update, and why a new object built on every render can cause updates you didn’t expect.

5. They treat text as text

This is the reason I’d add to the list. It saves teams from a whole class of security bugs without anyone thinking about it.

When you build UI by hand, the quick way to put a value into a page is innerHTML. It parses whatever string you give it as HTML. If that string came from a user, the user can write HTML into your page, including elements with event handlers that run their JavaScript under your domain. That attack is called cross-site scripting, or XSS.

const greeting = document.querySelector('#greeting');
const name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name') ?? '';
greeting.innerHTML = `Hi ${name}`;    // parses name as HTML
greeting.textContent = `Hi ${name}`;  // shows name as plain text

In React, <p>Hi {name}</p> always produces a text node, whatever name holds. Vue's {{ name }} and Angular's {{ name }} work the same way. To put raw HTML on the page you have to ask for it by name: React calls it dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue calls it v-html, and Angular runs anything bound to [innerHTML] through its sanitizer first. The safe way is the default, and the unsafe way is the one you have to go looking for.

6. They make a big codebase easier to work in

The first five points are things the library does at runtime. This one is about the people writing the code, and on a large team it may matter most of all.

  • Components. A <PriceTag> is written once, used in forty places, and changed in one file. With plain DOM code, "reuse" usually means copying a function and its HTML string into another file.
  • Clean-up has a home. Listeners you attach in the template (onClick, @click, (click)) are removed for you when the component goes away, and each library gives you one obvious place for the rest: the useEffect clean-up in React, onUnmounted in Vue, DestroyRef in Angular. By hand, every removeEventListener is yours to remember, and a forgotten one keeps the old element and everything it refers to in memory.
  • Tools that understand your app. React DevTools, Vue DevTools and Angular DevTools show your components and their current state, not just a tree of divs. Hot reload swaps an edited component while the page keeps running, often without losing what you typed into a form.
  • The editor catches mistakes. TypeScript checks JSX and Angular templates, so a misspelled prop or a wrong type shows up as you type, not as a blank screen.
  • A shared map. Routing, forms, data fetching and tests have well-known answers in each ecosystem. A new teammate who knows React already knows where state lives in your app and how a screen gets drawn. Hand-written DOM code is different in every company, and sometimes in every file.

When plain JavaScript is enough

None of this means every page needs a framework. This site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework at all. A blog post, a landing page, or a form with a couple of toggles has very little state and only a few places that show it, so the bugs from the first section rarely have room to happen.

A simple rule of thumb: reach for a library when the same data shows up in several parts of the screen and changes often. That’s where updating by hand starts to break, and where batching, skipping and safe defaults pay for the JavaScript you ship. Below that point, a few addEventListener calls and textContent are perfectly fine.

React, Vue and Angular are still DOM code. They call the same APIs you can. The difference is that they pick the moment, pick the cheap method, skip the pointless call and escape the dangerous string on every update, including the ones nobody on your team thought about.

All five demos (the two carts, the batching race, the innerText filter, the same-value counter and the innerHTML parser) run live here: https://allahabadi.dev/blogs/frontend/why-we-need-react-vue-angular/

corrida_no_ar.titulo: O que a ASICS prepara para o BRASIL e os NOVOS TÊNIS para 2027
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Em entrevista, Felipe Pontual, da ASICS Brasil, detalha a expansão da marca na América Latina, o sucesso da família Blast, o investimento em atletas de elite no Quênia e o forte apoio ao paratletismo brasileiro. Ele também adianta os planos e lançamentos para 2027, um ano…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Domingo | 1 de novembro de 2026

Para entender o que a ASICS tem feito no Brasil e quais os planos da marca para o futuro, Sérgio Rocha conversou com Felipe Pontual, gerente de comunicação e marca da ASICS Brasil, durante o TF Sports Summit 2026. Felipe, que antes atuava na área de sports marketing (o “Spoma”), agora cuida da comunicação e falou sobre a forte expansão da marca, o sucesso dos novos produtos e os investimentos em alto rendimento.

Expansão do circuito de provas

Felipe Pontual explicou que o escritório da ASICS no Brasil é o centro regional para toda a América Latina, o que permite a criação de uma estratégia consistente para a região. Um dos focos tem sido a expansão das provas de rua. A ASICS Golden Run, que já acontecia em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro, agora também tem etapas na Colômbia, Chile, Argentina e Peru. Além disso, foi criado o ASICS Run Challenge, um circuito pensado para regionalizar a presença da marca, levando corridas para outras praças importantes no Nordeste, Sul e Centro-Oeste do Brasil. “Tem para todo mundo, de distância e perfil”, comentou Felipe.

Renovação do portfólio: Família Blast e os clássicos

Um dos movimentos mais interessantes da ASICS nos últimos anos foi a renovação de sua linha de produtos. A marca conseguiu antever uma mudança no mercado e criou uma linha moderna e contemporânea para atender aos novos corredores, sem abandonar seus modelos clássicos. Segundo Felipe, a marca precisava se rejuvenescer. O grande ponto de virada foi o Novablast, que hoje já está em sua sexta edição e, de acordo com dados do Strava, se tornou o tênis mais usado no mundo. O sucesso foi tanto que deu origem à “família Blast”, com modelos como o Sonic Blast, Superblast e Megablast, cobrindo desde o iniciante até a alta performance. Ao mesmo tempo, a ASICS continua investindo em seus ícones, como o Nimbus, que vai para a 28ª edição, e o Kayano, que chegará à 33ª. “Não dá para soltar a mão da galera que tem muita história com o Nimbus, com o Kayano”, afirmou Felipe, mencionando que esses modelos agora também têm versões casuais, da linha Sportstyle.

Investimento no alto rendimento

A ASICS também tem feito um movimento forte para desafiar o monopólio de outras marcas no topo do pódio das grandes maratonas.
